item.title: 3 Years of Middle East Combat Altering How Navy Supplies, Maintains Fleet, Leaders Say
item.description: VIRGINIA BEACH, Va. — The ongoing U.S. conflict with Iran is morphing how the Navy fixes and supplies ships operating thousands of miles from logistics hubs as extended time at sea and the prospect of an extended naval commitment in the Middle East are creating a maintenance wave back home, service officials said this week. As of Monday, there were more than a dozen guided-missile destroyers supporting carriers USS George H.W. Bush (CVN-77) and USS George Washington (CVN-73) and the Boxer Amphibious Ready Group in the Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean, according to Monday’s USNI News Fleet and Marine Tracker.

item.description: MANILA, PHILIPPINES – An ex-Taiwan Coast Guard Administration patrol vessel is now under a Philippine flag in the most significant maritime security development between Taipei and Manila in recent years. item.description: North Korea test launched a new weapon over the weekend that appears to be a hypersonic missile, according to photos released Tuesday by state media Korean Central News Agency. KCNA did not specify what the weapons were but wording on a display of the missile’s movement reads: “Hwasongpho-11Ma-1 flight trajectory,” indicating an upgraded version of the Hwasong-11MA hypersonic missiles that North Korea unveiled last year. item.description: The following is the U.K.’s Defense Nuclear Enterprise 2026 Annual Update to Parliament, released Sept. 15, 2026. From the Report Introduction The UK’s nuclear deterrent, delivered since 1969 by the Royal Navy through Operation RELENTLESS, remains at the heart of our national security. To modernize and sustain the nuclear deterrent, the DNE is recapitalizing much of the enterprise simultaneously. item.title: Sixteen Years Ahead of His Time: Eni Faleomavaega’s Vision for American Samoa’s Ocean Future
item.description:
By 
by Michael J. McDonald,
American Pacific Resources

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — In American Samoa, we remember Congressman Eni Faleomavaega for many things: his decades of public service, his commanding voice in Washington, his advocacy for Pacific peoples, and his insistence that our small islands should never be treated as an afterthought in decisions affecting the Pacific.

But there is another part of Eni’s legacy that deserves renewed attention today.

More than fifteen years ago, Eni was asking a remarkably forward-looking question: What lies beneath the waters surrounding America and its Pacific territories— and shouldn’t we find out?

Today, in 2026, American Samoa is discussing a Proposed Leasing Notice from the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management for a potential offshore critical-minerals lease sale in federal waters near our islands.

The subject may seem new.

For Eni Faleomavaega, it was not.

HE SAW THE STRATEGIC IMPORTANCE EARLY

By 2010 and 2011, Eni was already raising concerns about seabed minerals and America's growing dependence on foreign sources of critical materials.

At a September 2011 congressional hearing examining China's dominance of rare earth minerals, Eni warned that America's dependence on China posed risks to both national security and economic well-being.

But he did more than identify the problem.

He asked whether America had taken the time to understand the resources potentially available within its own jurisdiction — including around the U.S. territories.

During that hearing, Eni specifically discussed the mineral wealth of the Pacific seabed, describing manganese nodules containing cobalt, manganese, copper and other elements distributed throughout the Pacific.

His own words are striking today. 

Speaking at the September 2011 hearing, Eni told his colleagues:

“We call it seabed minerals: Manganese nodules that contain cobalt, manganese, copper, so many other different rare elements, quite extensive throughout the Pacific region.”

He then identified what he believed was missing from the national discussion: “We have not done a very good job in putting our focus on this issue.”

His question was fundamentally one of knowledge: Do we actually know what we have? 
That question remains extraordinarily relevant sixteen years later.

ENI'S ANSWER WAS EXPLORATION AND SCIENCE

In 2011, Eni introduced H.R. 2803.

The legislation would have directed the Department of the Interior, acting through the federal offshore energy agency that preceded today's BOEM structure, to conduct a technological capability assessment, seabed survey and economic feasibility study regarding non-fuel minerals in America's shallow and deep seabed.

Importantly for us, his proposal specifically contemplated areas associated with the United States territories and possessions.

And this was not a subject Eni discovered in 2011. A year earlier, while chairing a congressional hearing on the South Pacific, he deliberately looked beyond the immediate issue of tuna and toward the long-term significance of the ocean itself.

He said, “I even understand in the Samoan Islands there is cobalt found there.” 

Then he explained the broader vision: “So not just fishing, tuna, but on a more long-term vision in terms of looking at these island countries, as small as they may be, beyond just fishing for tuna.”

And he put a direct question to the federal government:

“Does our Government have any interest in this area besides just tuna, the worth of manganese nodules in the seabeds of these island countries throughout the Pacific?”

Think about what that meant.

Eni was not proposing that America simply rush into the Pacific and start mining. He was proposing that America survey, assess, study and understand. 

Before making decisions about resources, we should first know what resources exist.

Before debating their economic potential, we should understand their characteristics.

Before deciding what should or should not happen in the future, we should develop the scientific information necessary to make an informed decision.

That distinction matters enormously today.

FROM 2011 TO 2026

Sixteen years later, the federal government is finally asking many of the questions Eni was raising.

BOEM's current process for American Samoa concerns a potential critical-minerals lease sale on the federal Outer Continental Shelf.

The Proposed Leasing Notice released in July is another step in that process. But a lease sale is not authorization to begin commercial mining.

BOEM itself explains that the environmental review conducted at this stage covers leasing and certain preliminary activities — surveys and activities intended to characterize the environment without significant adverse impacts to natural resources.

Any future testing, delineation or mining would require additional plans, federal approval and separate environmental review.

That distinction should be central to American Samoa's conversation.

Exploration is not mining.

Exploration is how we learn.

And remarkably, that is essentially where Eni began this conversation more than a decade and a half ago.

IMAGINE WHAT ENI WOULD ASK TODAY

None of us can say how Congressman Faleomavaega would view every aspect of today's BOEM process. We should not put words into the mouth of a leader who is no longer here to speak for himself.

But we do have his record.

And his record tells us the kinds of questions that interested him. 

What minerals exist?

Where are they?

What is their strategic importance?

Does America possess the technology to responsibly recover them?

What is their economic potential?

And what role should America's Pacific territories have in understanding resources located in the vast ocean areas surrounding them?

Those were sophisticated questions in 2011.

They are even more important in 2026.

KNOWLEDGE BEFORE CONCLUSIONS

American Samoa does not need to decide today whether deep-sea mining should someday occur near our islands.

There are still enormous scientific, environmental, cultural, technological and economic questions that must be answered.

But neither should we be afraid of acquiring the information necessary to answer them. There is a profound difference between studying a resource and exploiting it. Scientific exploration gives us knowledge. 

Environmental research gives us baselines. 

Mapping tells us what is actually there.

And participation in the federal process gives American Samoa an opportunity to insist that our interests, culture, ocean traditions and economic aspirations are understood before decisions affecting our region are made.

We should approach this process carefully. We should demand strong environmental safeguards. We should insist upon transparency.

We should listen to fishermen, scientists, traditional leaders, environmental advocates, young people and our communities.

But we should also continue learning.

Because decisions made without knowledge are not necessarily more protective than decisions made with it.

ENI WAS LOOKING BEYOND THE HORIZON

Perhaps that is the most remarkable part of revisiting Eni Faleomavaega's words today.

In 2010 and 2011, deep-seabed critical minerals were hardly part of the everyday political conversation in American Samoa.

China's dominance of critical-mineral supply chains was not yet the major national-security issue it has become today.

And a federal critical-minerals leasing process near American Samoa probably seemed distant. Yet Eni was already looking beyond the horizon.

In fact, the phrase he used in 2010—“a more long-term vision”—may be the best description of what his record represents today.

He understood that the Pacific was not simply an empty blue space between continents.

He understood that the ocean surrounding Pacific islands held scientific, strategic and potentially economic significance that the United States had barely begun to understand.

And he believed America should find out what was there.

Now, sixteen years later, American Samoa finds itself standing at almost exactly that doorway. We do not yet know where it leads. And we certainly do not have to predetermine the destination.

But perhaps Eni's vision offers us some guidance about how to begin: Explore. Study. Document. Understand.

Then, armed with knowledge rather than speculation, make informed decisions about the future. 

That was a remarkably forward-looking idea in 2011.

In 2026, it may be more relevant than ever.

(Editor’s Note: In the spirit of transparency, Samoa News notes that Michael J. McDonald is an Assistant Director of the American Samoa Port Administration. He is the Senior Advisor on deep-sea and critical minerals matters, and also serves as the chairman of the ASG Deep-Sea Minerals Steering Committee.)

The Proposed Leasing Notice released in July is another step in that process. But a lease sale is not authorization to begin commercial mining.
BOEM itself explains that the environmental review conducted at this stage covers leasing and certain preliminary activities — surveys and activities intended to characterize the environment without significant adverse impacts to natural resources.
Any future testing, delineation or mining would require additional plans, federal approval and separate environmental review.
That distinction should be central to American Samoa's conversation.
Exploration is not mining.
Exploration is how we learn.
And remarkably, that is essentially where Eni began this conversation more than a decade and a half ago.
**IMAGINE WHAT ENI WOULD ASK TODAY**
None of us can say how Congressman Faleomavaega would view every aspect of today's BOEM process. We should not put words into the mouth of a leader who is no longer here to speak for himself.
But we do have his record.
And his record tells us the kinds of questions that interested him.
What minerals exist?
Where are they?
What is their strategic importance?
Does America possess the technology to responsibly recover them?
What is their economic potential?
And what role should America's Pacific territories have in understanding resources located in the vast ocean areas surrounding them?
Those were sophisticated questions in 2011.
They are even more important in 2026.
**KNOWLEDGE BEFORE CONCLUSIONS**
American Samoa does not need to decide today whether deep-sea mining should someday occur near our islands.
There are still enormous scientific, environmental, cultural, technological and economic questions that must be answered.
But neither should we be afraid of acquiring the information necessary to answer them. There is a profound difference between studying a resource and exploiting it. Scientific exploration gives us knowledge.
Environmental research gives us baselines.
Mapping tells us what is actually there.
And participation in the federal process gives American Samoa an opportunity to insist that our interests, culture, ocean traditions and economic aspirations are understood before decisions affecting our region are made.
We should approach this process carefully. We should demand strong environmental safeguards. We should insist upon transparency.
We should listen to fishermen, scientists, traditional leaders, environmental advocates, young people and our communities.
But we should also continue learning.
Because decisions made without knowledge are not necessarily more protective than decisions made with it.
**ENI WAS LOOKING BEYOND THE HORIZON**
Perhaps that is the most remarkable part of revisiting Eni Faleomavaega's words today.
In 2010 and 2011, deep-seabed critical minerals were hardly part of the everyday political conversation in American Samoa.
China's dominance of critical-mineral supply chains was not yet the major national-security issue it has become today.
And a federal critical-minerals leasing process near American Samoa probably seemed distant. Yet Eni was already looking beyond the horizon.
In fact, the phrase he used in 2010—“a more long-term vision”—may be the best description of what his record represents today.
He understood that the Pacific was not simply an empty blue space between continents.
He understood that the ocean surrounding Pacific islands held scientific, strategic and potentially economic significance that the United States had barely begun to understand.
And he believed America should find out what was there.
Now, sixteen years later, American Samoa finds itself standing at almost exactly that doorway. We do not yet know where it leads. And we certainly do not have to predetermine the destination.
But perhaps Eni's vision offers us some guidance about how to begin: Explore. Study. Document. Understand.
Then, armed with knowledge rather than speculation, make informed decisions about the future.
That was a remarkably forward-looking idea in 2011.
In 2026, it may be more relevant than ever.
_(Editor’s Note: In the spirit of transparency, Samoa News notes that Michael J. McDonald is an Assistant Director of the American Samoa Port Administration. He is the Senior Advisor on deep-sea and critical minerals matters, and also serves as the chairman of the ASG Deep-Sea Minerals Steering Committee.)_

item.title: U.S. Destroyer Practices Underway Refueling with Seahawk USV
item.description: A U.S. destroyer refueled an Unmanned Surface Vessel earlier this month in the Pacific as part of the Navy’s latest development effort to hone at-sea drone sustainment, the sea service announced Monday. USS Chafee (DDG-90) conducted an at-sea fueling of Seahawk, a Medium Displacement USV on Sept. 11, according to photos released Monday by the Navy. The astern refueling method was previously tested between Seahawk and oiler USNS Guadalupe (T-AO 200) in April. The April refueling of the MDUSV was “critical to deployed operations of MUSVs in conjunction with a carrier strike group,” Military Sealift Command said in a statement

item.title: Senate passes Anti‑Kickback Prohibition Act of 2026
item.description:
Moves to House
By 
Asi Andrew Fa'asau
andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The Senate has unanimously approved legislation creating the Anti‑Kickback Prohibition Act of 2026, a measure aimed at closing long‑standing gaps in procurement oversight and establishing a uniform, enforceable standard across all government entities.

According to the bill’s preamble, while certain anti‑kickback protections already exist in administrative rules and within the Procurement Act, no comprehensive, territory‑wide prohibition currently governs kickbacks, gratuities, or referral fees across all agencies and public corporations. Lawmakers say the absence of a unified standard has left room for inconsistent practices and vulnerabilities in government contracting.

The bill states that it is therefore necessary to consolidate, strengthen, and expand existing protections to ensure that government agencies, vendors, contractors, and subcontractors operate under a single, clear, and enforceable framework.

The Act establishes broad prohibitions covering every stage of government contracting. It specifies that no person may provide, offer, solicit, request, or accept any kickback, gratuity, or referral fee connected to the award of a government contract, the extension, modification, or renewal of a government contract, any procurement‑related recommendation, evaluation, or decision,  and any official action taken by a covered individual.

The bill further prohibits indirect payments made through intermediaries, affiliates, subcontractors, or related parties for the purpose of influencing government action.

KEY CONCEPT: KICKBACK VIOLATIONS

Individuals are also barred from requesting or accepting any kickback or gratuity from vendors, contractors, subcontractors, or any person seeking or performing government work.

Subcontractors are explicitly prohibited from making payments to contractors or other subcontractors to secure a subcontract award or favorable treatment under a government contract.

To strengthen transparency, the Act requires all bids, proposals, and contract submissions to disclose any commissions, fees, or compensation arrangements with third parties, any ownership, familial, or financial relationship with a covered individual, any subcontractor or intermediary receiving compensation related to the bid, and any contingent fee arrangement.

Failure to disclose required information may result in disqualification, contract termination, suspension or debarment, and civil penalties.

The bill includes provisions for reporting suspected violations and offers whistleblower protections to individuals who come forward with information.

Penalties for violations include contract termination, suspension or debarment, a $25,000 fine per violation, recovery of improperly obtained funds, voiding of contracts secured through prohibited conduct.

These measures aim to deter misconduct and ensure that government procurement processes remain fair, transparent, and accountable.

The bill, sponsored by Senator Togiola T.A. Tulafono, now moves to the House of Representatives for review.

If approved by both the House and the Governor, the Anti‑Kickback Prohibition Act of 2026 would take effect 90 days after the Governor signs it.

 

Section: 
Local News
Tags: 
Anti‑Kickback Prohibition Act of 2026

item.title: U.S. Army Contracts First Batch of Maritime Precision Strike Missiles
item.description: The U.S. Army contracted the first batch of Precision Strike Missiles designed to strike moving maritime targets last week. Lockheed Martin was awarded $1.2 billion by the ground branch for work on the early operational capability munitions of PrSM Increment 2, a variant that integrates a new seeker capable of mobile targets, the Pentagon announced on Sept. 14. Work is expected to be completed by September of 2031, reads the Pentagon’s contracts page. The procurement of the maritime strike PrSM variant was slated to begin within Fiscal Year 2026, according to the Army’s Justification Book covering missile procurement. PrSM Inc.

item.title: Steves: In Europe, make your memento-shopping memorable
item.description:
With each trip I take, I look for cultural souvenirs — experiences and memories are the gold nuggets of travel. Shopping is never my priority, but when I do bring mementos home I find the best souvenirs come from local entrepreneurs and craftspeople. These days, Europe’s modern shopping arenas are also fun spots to witness a slice of contemporary life. In moderation, it can be fun to immerse yourself in the retail culture of Europe’s grandest cities.

The post Steves: In Europe, make your memento-shopping memorable appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Carrier USS Abraham Lincoln Pulls into Guam for Logistics Stop, Deployment Now at 302 Days
item.description: Carrier USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72), the embarked Carrier Air Wing 9 and the guided-missile destroyer USS Frank Petersen (DDG-121) pulled into Guam on Saturday, according to a statement from U.S. 7th Fleet. Lincoln exited the South China Sea this week via the Sulu Sea, according to ship spotters, and arrived at Apra Harbor for a logistics stop. “The stop on Naval Base Guam marks [Carrier Strike Group]-3 personnel’s first return to American soil in nine months, during which personnel will be afforded on-base liberty,” reads the statement. The post visit to Guam follows the carrier’s port visit to Pattaya, Thailand

item.title: Zoning Board’s role and enforcement authority question by lawmakers
item.description:
By 
Asi Andrew Fa'asau
andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Lawmakers are questioning the role and enforcement authority of the American Samoa Zoning Board after raising concerns that some business owners are operating multiple ventures within a single location in violation of zoning and licensing rules.

The concerns surfaced Wednesday during the Fono’s joint budget hearings as legislators reviewed the FY 2027 proposed budget for the Department of Commerce (DOC). Appearing before the committee were DOC Deputy Director Uili Leauanae, Assistant Deputy Director for Urban Planning & Development Reinette V. Thompson‑Niko, and Comptroller Lorina Ofagalilo.

During the hearing, Rep. Faimealelei Anthony Allen pressed the DOC officials on whether the department conducts on‑site inspections before issuing business licenses. He argued that the lack of physical inspections has allowed some business owners to operate multiple, unrelated ventures within the same compound — arrangements he said violate zoning classifications and create public safety concerns.

Faimealelei pointed to examples where restaurants were operating alongside carwash services, with vehicles being washed just steps away from dining areas. He said such setups raise questions about sanitation, safety, and whether the businesses were ever properly vetted.

The Aua faipule also highlighted O&O Enterprises in Nu‘uuli, which he said operates a retail store, wholesale outlet, and car rental service all within the same location. He argued that clustering these operations into one site has created significant parking shortages and contributed to traffic congestion along the adjacent main road.

“With all these business operations crammed into one location, there is not enough parking space for customers,” Faimealelei said. “It’s causing traffic delays and congestion right next to the main road.”

Faimealelei questioned how such businesses were able to obtain licenses in the first place.

“How did this happen?” he asked. “How did these businesses receive licenses from your department to run their operations with blatant disregard for existing laws?”

In response, Deputy Director Uili Leauanae told lawmakers that business license applications — particularly for operations like the one in Nuʻuuli — are required to demonstrate adequate parking space before they can be considered. 

He noted that Nuʻuuli falls within the Territory’s Watershed Conservation Zone, a zoning category where commercial activity is generally prohibited. Because of this, any business proposal in the area must be forwarded to the Zoning Board for special review.

Leauanae explained that the Zoning Board evaluates two key factors: whether the proposed parking layout meets the mandated setback distance from the main road, and whether the business itself aligns with the zoning laws governing the area. Only after the Board determines that the proposal satisfies zoning requirements does the Department of Commerce issue a business license.

He emphasized that the Zoning Board operates as an independent authority within the Department of Commerce. The Board consists of nine members: four appointed by the Governor from the Executive Branch; three appointed by the District Governors through the Office of Local Government; and two representing the Legislature, appointed by the Senate President and the Speaker of the House.

Representative Ben Sauvao raised concerns over the Port Administration’s plan to construct a large‑scale solar farm on airport property, a project slated for the grassy area at the end of the runway as part of the Vision 2030 redevelopment initiative. The solar installation is expected to generate between 20 and 24 megawatts of power, making it one of the largest renewable‑energy projects ever undertaken in American Samoa.

Sauvao, who represents Tualauta, said the proposed location sits uncomfortably close to the main road and to residential homes in his district. He also pointed out its proximity to the Tafuna High School compound, noting that any major infrastructure project of this scale warrants careful review to ensure the safety and well‑being of nearby residents and students.

The Tualauta faipule asked DOC officials whether a land‑use permit application for the solar farm had been submitted and, if so, whether it had been referred to the Zoning Board for mandatory review. Sauvao added that he was aware a contractor had already been awarded the project, raising questions about whether zoning procedures were being followed in the correct order.

Deputy Director Leauanae responded that he was not certain whether an application had been filed with the department. He assured lawmakers that he would check the status of the permit and report back to the Fono.

In an exclusive interview with Zoning Board Acting Chairman Motuiliu Vesi Matuʻu, he recalled that the land-use permit for the O&O Enterprises businesses in Nu'uuli was allegedly approved more than 20 years ago. 

O&O Enterprises submitted its most recent land‑use permit application in October 2025, proposing the construction of a shopping center on four acres of individually owned land behind the Veterans Memorial Stadium in Tafuna. 

The property, leased from Domina Louata Kellog and her brother Harold Fonoti Annastas, borders a residential neighborhood in Petesa, just past the School Lunch Program Office. The initial site plan proposed an entry point on the Petesa side, placing commercial traffic directly into the residential area.

Motuiliu said the Zoning Board rejected that portion of the proposal to prevent traffic congestion and protect the quiet‑use character of the Petesa neighborhood. The Board ruled that any access road for the shopping center must instead branch off the airport road next to the stadium, where traffic flow is better suited to commercial activity.

The Acting Chair, who serves as the Western District Governor’s representative on the Board, as well as its Deputy Chairman, reiterated that adequate parking remains a critical prerequisite for any land‑use permit application. He said parking availability directly affects traffic flow, pedestrian safety, and emergency access — especially in high‑congestion areas such as Nuʻuuli, where O&O’s existing operations have already drawn scrutiny from lawmakers. 

Without a detailed parking plan, he noted, the Board cannot determine whether a proposed development meets zoning requirements or protects surrounding communities. Without a clear plan demonstrating how customer and employee vehicles would be accommodated, he said the Board could not legally approve the request.

Motuiliu emphasized that the Board’s decision does not end the matter entirely. Under zoning procedures, O&O Enterprises retains the right to appeal the denial, allowing the applicant to present additional information or request reconsideration if they believe the Board erred or if new documentation becomes available.

Regarding the Port Administration’s proposed solar farm on airport property, Motuiliu stated that the Zoning Board has not received any land‑use permit application for the project. He noted that, given the scale of the proposed 20‑ to 24‑megawatt installation and its proximity to residential neighborhoods, Tafuna High School, and the main road, a zoning review would be required before any construction could legally proceed. The absence of an application, he said, indicates that the project has not yet entered the zoning approval process.

Faipule Faimealelei told the joint budget hearing that he intends to call the American Samoa Zoning Board before the House of Representatives to explain how certain businesses were allowed to operate despite blatantly violating zoning laws. 

He acknowledged that it was clear previous boards had approved land‑use permit applications for these businesses, and said he would formally request access to the Board’s meeting minutes — records which, by law, should be preserved in the national archives.

Faimealelei said the Legislature needs to understand how these approvals were granted, particularly in cases where businesses were operating multiple ventures on a single property without meeting zoning requirements for parking, access roads, or land‑use compatibility. He emphasized that reviewing past minutes is essential to determining whether proper procedures were followed or whether oversight failures occurred.

The current members of the American Samoa Zoning Board include Chairman Vesiai Poyer Samuelu (Governor’s appointee); Assistant Attorney General Louise Lafitaga, who serves as the Board’s legal counsel; Puletu Dick Koko (Governor’s appointee); Rep. Ape M. Asifoa (House Speaker’s appointee); James L. McGuire (Senate President’s appointee); Tavita Tili (Manu‘a District Governor’s appointee); Taesali Lefiti (Governor’s appointee); Motuiliu Vesi Matuʻu (Western District Governor’s appointee); Taesali Matagi (Eastern District Governor’s appointee); and Fofoga Sagato (Governor’s appointee).

Members of the American Samoa Zoning Board during their meeting last week. From left: Puletu Dick Koko, Rep. Ape M. Asifoa, Vesiai Poyer Samuelu (Chairman), ZB Legal Counsel Assistant AG Louise Lafitaga, James L. McGuire, Tavita Tili, and Taesali Lefiti. Absent: Motuiliu Vesi Matu'u, Taesali Matagi, Fofoga Sagato. [photo: Asi A. Fa'asau]

With the Board now under heightened scrutiny, Faimealelei said the upcoming hearing will focus on understanding the decision‑making process behind past approvals, ensuring compliance with zoning laws, and determining whether corrective action is needed to prevent similar violations in the future.

The Zoning Board is responsible for regulating land use across the Territory under Title 26, Chapter 3 of the American Samoa Code Annotated (A.S.C.A.). It ensures that development is safe, orderly, and consistent with zoning laws.

Among its mandated roles, the Zoning Board controls intensity of use where multi‑use or high‑traffic businesses may be restricted if the zone cannot support parking, traffic flow, or safety requirements. It also governs mixed-use operations where applications for running multiple businesses on one property often require special approval or a Planned Unit Development (PUD).

If the land use doesn’t match the business activity, DOC cannot legally issue a license unless the Zoning Board approves a variance or reclassification.

Of note, not mentioned during the joint hearing is that another over-crowded business area in Nuuuli, is located just up the road from O&O, right next to the Catholic church. It is home to the Tuinaitau car rental, a game center, laundromat, and retail store — they all share the same parking lot to the front of the main building in the locale, which is right off the main road. 

The business started out as a locally owned mom & pop store, and was then taken over by Asians that now operate multiple businesses out of the location. 

There has also been questions in the community about the new two-story building that was added in the location that seems to be a flimsy-looking pre-fab. It houses the game center on the bottom and what looks like living quarters on the top floor.

[![The four‑acre parcel ](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/slideshow/public/field/image/6380.jpg?itok=wTBrEJl1)](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/article_normal_image/public/field/image/6380.jpg?itok=ZyQsmS5p)
By
Asi Andrew Fa'asau
andrew@samoanews.com
_Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA —_ Lawmakers are questioning the role and enforcement authority of the American Samoa Zoning Board after raising concerns that some business owners are operating multiple ventures within a single location in violation of zoning and licensing rules.
The concerns surfaced Wednesday during the Fono’s joint budget hearings as legislators reviewed the FY 2027 proposed budget for the Department of Commerce (DOC). Appearing before the committee were DOC Deputy Director Uili Leauanae, Assistant Deputy Director for Urban Planning & Development Reinette V. Thompson‑Niko, and Comptroller Lorina Ofagalilo.
During the hearing, Rep. Faimealelei Anthony Allen pressed the DOC officials on whether the department conducts on‑site inspections before issuing business licenses. He argued that the lack of physical inspections has allowed some business owners to operate multiple, unrelated ventures within the same compound — arrangements he said violate zoning classifications and create public safety concerns.
Faimealelei pointed to examples where restaurants were operating alongside carwash services, with vehicles being washed just steps away from dining areas. He said such setups raise questions about sanitation, safety, and whether the businesses were ever properly vetted.
The Aua faipule also highlighted O&O Enterprises in Nu‘uuli, which he said operates a retail store, wholesale outlet, and car rental service all within the same location. He argued that clustering these operations into one site has created significant parking shortages and contributed to traffic congestion along the adjacent main road.
“With all these business operations crammed into one location, there is not enough parking space for customers,” Faimealelei said. “It’s causing traffic delays and congestion right next to the main road.”
Faimealelei questioned how such businesses were able to obtain licenses in the first place.
“How did this happen?” he asked. “How did these businesses receive licenses from your department to run their operations with blatant disregard for existing laws?”
In response, Deputy Director Uili Leauanae told lawmakers that business license applications — particularly for operations like the one in Nuʻuuli — are required to demonstrate adequate parking space before they can be considered.
He noted that Nuʻuuli falls within the Territory’s Watershed Conservation Zone, a zoning category where commercial activity is generally prohibited. Because of this, any business proposal in the area must be forwarded to the Zoning Board for special review.
Leauanae explained that the Zoning Board evaluates two key factors: whether the proposed parking layout meets the mandated setback distance from the main road, and whether the business itself aligns with the zoning laws governing the area. Only after the Board determines that the proposal satisfies zoning requirements does the Department of Commerce issue a business license.
He emphasized that the Zoning Board operates as an independent authority within the Department of Commerce. The Board consists of nine members: four appointed by the Governor from the Executive Branch; three appointed by the District Governors through the Office of Local Government; and two representing the Legislature, appointed by the Senate President and the Speaker of the House.
Representative Ben Sauvao raised concerns over the Port Administration’s plan to construct a large‑scale solar farm on airport property, a project slated for the grassy area at the end of the runway as part of the Vision 2030 redevelopment initiative. The solar installation is expected to generate between 20 and 24 megawatts of power, making it one of the largest renewable‑energy projects ever undertaken in American Samoa.
Sauvao, who represents Tualauta, said the proposed location sits uncomfortably close to the main road and to residential homes in his district. He also pointed out its proximity to the Tafuna High School compound, noting that any major infrastructure project of this scale warrants careful review to ensure the safety and well‑being of nearby residents and students.
The Tualauta faipule asked DOC officials whether a land‑use permit application for the solar farm had been submitted and, if so, whether it had been referred to the Zoning Board for mandatory review. Sauvao added that he was aware a contractor had already been awarded the project, raising questions about whether zoning procedures were being followed in the correct order.
Deputy Director Leauanae responded that he was not certain whether an application had been filed with the department. He assured lawmakers that he would check the status of the permit and report back to the Fono.
In an exclusive interview with Zoning Board Acting Chairman Motuiliu Vesi Matuʻu, he recalled that the land-use permit for the O&O Enterprises businesses in Nu'uuli was allegedly approved more than 20 years ago.
O&O Enterprises submitted its most recent land‑use permit application in October 2025, proposing the construction of a shopping center on four acres of individually owned land behind the Veterans Memorial Stadium in Tafuna.
The property, leased from Domina Louata Kellog and her brother Harold Fonoti Annastas, borders a residential neighborhood in Petesa, just past the School Lunch Program Office. The initial site plan proposed an entry point on the Petesa side, placing commercial traffic directly into the residential area.
Motuiliu said the Zoning Board rejected that portion of the proposal to prevent traffic congestion and protect the quiet‑use character of the Petesa neighborhood. The Board ruled that any access road for the shopping center must instead branch off the airport road next to the stadium, where traffic flow is better suited to commercial activity.
The Acting Chair, who serves as the Western District Governor’s representative on the Board, as well as its Deputy Chairman, reiterated that adequate parking remains a critical prerequisite for any land‑use permit application. He said parking availability directly affects traffic flow, pedestrian safety, and emergency access — especially in high‑congestion areas such as Nuʻuuli, where O&O’s existing operations have already drawn scrutiny from lawmakers.
Without a detailed parking plan, he noted, the Board cannot determine whether a proposed development meets zoning requirements or protects surrounding communities. Without a clear plan demonstrating how customer and employee vehicles would be accommodated, he said the Board could not legally approve the request.
Motuiliu emphasized that the Board’s decision does not end the matter entirely. Under zoning procedures, O&O Enterprises retains the right to appeal the denial, allowing the applicant to present additional information or request reconsideration if they believe the Board erred or if new documentation becomes available.
Regarding the Port Administration’s proposed solar farm on airport property, Motuiliu stated that the Zoning Board has not received any land‑use permit application for the project. He noted that, given the scale of the proposed 20‑ to 24‑megawatt installation and its proximity to residential neighborhoods, Tafuna High School, and the main road, a zoning review would be required before any construction could legally proceed. The absence of an application, he said, indicates that the project has not yet entered the zoning approval process.
Faipule Faimealelei told the joint budget hearing that he intends to call the American Samoa Zoning Board before the House of Representatives to explain how certain businesses were allowed to operate despite blatantly violating zoning laws.
He acknowledged that it was clear previous boards had approved land‑use permit applications for these businesses, and said he would formally request access to the Board’s meeting minutes — records which, by law, should be preserved in the national archives.
Faimealelei said the Legislature needs to understand how these approvals were granted, particularly in cases where businesses were operating multiple ventures on a single property without meeting zoning requirements for parking, access roads, or land‑use compatibility. He emphasized that reviewing past minutes is essential to determining whether proper procedures were followed or whether oversight failures occurred.
The current members of the American Samoa Zoning Board include Chairman Vesiai Poyer Samuelu (Governor’s appointee); Assistant Attorney General Louise Lafitaga, who serves as the Board’s legal counsel; Puletu Dick Koko (Governor’s appointee); Rep. Ape M. Asifoa (House Speaker’s appointee); James L. McGuire (Senate President’s appointee); Tavita Tili (Manu‘a District Governor’s appointee); Taesali Lefiti (Governor’s appointee); Motuiliu Vesi Matuʻu (Western District Governor’s appointee); Taesali Matagi (Eastern District Governor’s appointee); and Fofoga Sagato (Governor’s appointee).

item.title: Isolated Kauai residents remain resilient despite hazards left by Lowell
item.description:
WAINIHA, Kauai — As many Kauai residents begin to return to a sense of normalcy following Hurricane Lowell, those who live in one of the island’s most isolated communities continue to drive underneath trees suspended from power lines.

item.title: Navy Wants Containerized, Low-cost Interceptors to Defeat Cruise Missiles, Drones
item.description: The U.S. Navy wants to deploy containerized low-cost interceptors to defeat cruise missiles and attack drones, according to a request for white papers released Wednesday. Dubbed the Naval Affordable Interceptor, the concept seeks to field a container launcher that can carry at least 60 missiles. The system’s installation should not require permanent modification aboard its host warship. Interested firms should be able to produce 500 interceptors annually and operationally deploy the system within 12 months of award. The white paper’s request and requirements for the low-cost interceptors are for the first system planned to be procured by the Navy’s Portfolio

item.title: Governor submits formal comments on proposed federal offshore mineral lease sale
item.description:
“Learn first. Protect what sustains us. Make informed decisions.”
Source: ASG press release

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Governor Pulaali‘i Nikolao Pula has submitted his formal comments to the U.S. Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) regarding the proposed PACM-1 offshore mineral lease sale.

The Governor’s comments were informed by public comments submitted to his office, the work of the Deep-Sea Minerals Steering Committee, input from territorial agencies and subject-matter experts, and the views, concerns, and perspectives on deep-sea minerals that members of the community have shared publicly over the past year.

Governor Pulaali‘i thanks the many members of the community who took the time to submit comments, ask questions, share information, and express their concerns and perspectives. He also recognizes the members of the Steering Committee, territorial agencies, and subject-matter experts whose contributions helped inform his final comments.

“Our people care deeply about our ocean and what we leave for future generations,” he said. “I have listened carefully to the concerns being raised, particularly about our fisheries and marine environment. Those concerns matter, and they are reflected in the position I have submitted to the Federal Government.”

The Governor’s comments make clear that American Samoa does not support commercial deep-sea mineral extraction at this time. Significant questions remain about the potential effects of large-scale extraction on deep-ocean ecosystems, fisheries, and the broader marine environment.

At the same time, Governor Pulaali‘i recognizes that the proposed lease areas are in federal waters outside American Samoa’s territorial jurisdiction and that the decision whether to proceed with the lease sale rests with the United States Government. His comments therefore focus on protecting American Samoa’s interests and ensuring that the Territory remains fully engaged as the federal process moves forward.

A central message of the Governor’s submission is that the current lease process should not be confused with authorization to commercially mine the seafloor. 

If the Federal Government proceeds, Preliminary Activities should be used to gather credible science, establish environmental baselines, better understand potential impacts, and provide information needed for future decisions. Any later proposal for commercial extraction must be treated as a separate decision and undergo the environmental, scientific, regulatory, and governmental review required at that time.

The Governor’s comments also call for strong fisheries protections, environmental monitoring and transparency, protection of Rose Atoll and other marine resources, safeguards for territorial infrastructure, meaningful opportunities for American Samoa workers and businesses, workforce development, and an equitable share for American Samoa of revenues that could result from any future offshore mineral development.

For members of the community who remain concerned about the process, Governor Pulaali‘i emphasized that no decision on commercial mining is being made today. The current process provides an opportunity to learn more, strengthen protections, and ensure that American Samoa’s interests are represented before decisions about any future commercial activity are considered.

“We should not be afraid to learn more, and we should not be pressured to decide our future before we have the information needed to make that decision,” he said. “We will remain engaged, protect what sustains our people, and insist that American Samoa’s voice is heard.”

The Governor’s comments conclude with a simple principle for American Samoa’s approach:

“Learn first. Protect what sustains us. Make informed decisions.”

 

Section: 
Local News
Tags: 
deep sea mining

item.title: Marines Test USV for Littoral Explosive Ordnance Disposal Operations
item.description: The Marine Corps trialled using an Unmanned Surface Vessel as part of its Littoral Explosive Ordnance Neutralization System last month. The USV trials were carried out by Program Manager Combat Support Systems (PM CSS) of Portfolio Acquisition Executive Marine Corps (PAE MC) with a PM CSS Explosive Hazard Defeat Team at Camp Pendleton, Calif. The trials were held in response to a littoral capability gap with the solution being a commercial USV equipped with integrated autonomous driving and payloads that consist of Sonar, Forward-Looking Infrared cameras, Line of Sight Communications and Acoustic Communications (AComms), reads a PAE MC news release

The UAS, assigned to the 502nd Squadron, Air Warning Wing based at JASDF Misawa Air Base, took off at 10:20 a.m. local time on Tuesday, according to a JASDF report on the loss. There was a communication failure with the Global Hawk around 12:55 p.m. and the drone disappeared from radar

item.title: Former and current ASTCA board members pressed on questions about spending on the American250 festivities
item.description:
New revelations come to light about ASTCA COO Chuck Leota’s severance payout
By 
Asi Andrew Fa'asau
andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Former and current members of the American Samoa Telecommunications Authority (ASTCA) appeared before the Senate Government Operations Committee Monday, where lawmakers examined how ASTCA funds were used during the American250 celebrations — and confronted new revelation that ASTCA money was used to make a child support payment for former CEO and current Chief Operations Officer Chuck Leota, without board approval.

Committee Chairman Sen. Togiola T.A. Tulafono opened the hearing by noting widespread public concern over what many view as excessive spending on the American250 festivities. He emphasized that the Fono had not appropriated any specific funding for ASTCA to participate in the celebrations.

Former board chairman Avamua Dave Haleck, former vice chairman Maota Alex Sene, former second vice chair Ella Gurr, and former board secretary Andrew Berquist testified alongside current board members Omar Shalhout (acting chairman), Lewis Seau, Karen Satele, and Molitogi Lemana.

Avamua, who resigned from the board in July 2026 after the celebrations, said he stepped down to focus on his family businesses. When pressed by Togiola and Senate President Tuaolo Manaia Fruean on whether other factors influenced his resignation, he repeatedly stated that business and family obligations were the only reasons.

Avamua and Maota explained that the American250 budget was drawn from ASTCA’s FY2026 marketing allocation, which totaled just over $1 million. They said that once the budget was approved, the ASTCA CEO had full authority to spend the funds.

The CEO presented the celebration plans to the board, and ASTCA funded the event in partnership with The Reid Group, with additional contributions from other government departments.

When asked how much of the marketing budget was earmarked for the celebrations, Avamua said the CEO informed the board that between $200,000 and $300,000 would be spent.

Senator Togiola sought confirmation that board minutes existed documenting approval for the American250 spending. Former board secretary Andrew Berquist said he no longer had access to the email drive containing the minutes because he rescinded his access after resigning.

He said the electronic records were turned over to ASTCA legal counsel William Ledoux, who currently resides off‑island, and board member Lewis Seau. Togiola requested that the committee be provided with all minutes related to the American250 discussions.

CHILD SUPPORT PAYMENT BY ASTCA

The hearing took a sharp turn when Senate President Tuaolo asked Avamua whether the board had approved $100,000 for a child support payment made on behalf of former CEO Chuck Leota to the High Court.

Avamua confirmed the payment had been made — but insisted it was not the reason he resigned.

Tuaolo pressed further: “Who approved it? Did the board approve $100,000 for Chuck’s child support?”

Former vice chair Ella Gurr responded. She explained that Leota’s severance package was under discussion, and the board had considered transitioning him into a career service position as Chief Operations Officer instead of issuing a severance payout.

She said the child support payment was raised during board discussions, but the majority of the board did not support it, and the matter was tabled.

According to Gurr, the ASTCA CEO then sought approval directly from the Governor, who approved the payment. The board only learned about it afterward.

Tuaolo asked again whether the board had approved the payment. Avamua confirmed:

“No, the board did not approve it.”

He also confirmed that the Governor had approved the payment.

Senator Togiola asked where the money came from. Avamua said the payment was issued from ASTCA’s general account, and the check was made out to the High Court of American Samoa.

Samoa News will report further in tomorrow’s issue on ASTCA CEO Folasaitu Sorepa Thomas’ answers to direct questioning that took place on Monday morning during the Fono’s joint budget hearing regarding the controversial child support payment made on behalf of former CEO Chuck Leota using ASTCA funds.

item.source:markdown:
New revelations come to light about ASTCA COO Chuck Leota’s severance payout
[![Former and current members of ASTCA board](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/slideshow/public/field/image/img_7302.jpg?itok=37hw-ASv)](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/article_normal_image/public/field/image/img_7302.jpg?itok=roji4gr_)
By
Asi Andrew Fa'asau
andrew@samoanews.com
_Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA —_ Former and current members of the American Samoa Telecommunications Authority (ASTCA) appeared before the Senate Government Operations Committee Monday, where lawmakers examined how ASTCA funds were used during the American250 celebrations — and confronted new revelation that ASTCA money was used to make a child support payment for former CEO and current Chief Operations Officer Chuck Leota, without board approval.
Committee Chairman Sen. Togiola T.A. Tulafono opened the hearing by noting widespread public concern over what many view as excessive spending on the American250 festivities. He emphasized that the Fono had not appropriated any specific funding for ASTCA to participate in the celebrations.
Former board chairman Avamua Dave Haleck, former vice chairman Maota Alex Sene, former second vice chair Ella Gurr, and former board secretary Andrew Berquist testified alongside current board members Omar Shalhout (acting chairman), Lewis Seau, Karen Satele, and Molitogi Lemana.
Avamua, who resigned from the board in July 2026 after the celebrations, said he stepped down to focus on his family businesses. When pressed by Togiola and Senate President Tuaolo Manaia Fruean on whether other factors influenced his resignation, he repeatedly stated that business and family obligations were the only reasons.
Avamua and Maota explained that the American250 budget was drawn from ASTCA’s FY2026 marketing allocation, which totaled just over $1 million. They said that once the budget was approved, the ASTCA CEO had full authority to spend the funds.
The CEO presented the celebration plans to the board, and ASTCA funded the event in partnership with The Reid Group, with additional contributions from other government departments.
When asked how much of the marketing budget was earmarked for the celebrations, Avamua said the CEO informed the board that between $200,000 and $300,000 would be spent.
Senator Togiola sought confirmation that board minutes existed documenting approval for the American250 spending. Former board secretary Andrew Berquist said he no longer had access to the email drive containing the minutes because he rescinded his access after resigning.
He said the electronic records were turned over to ASTCA legal counsel William Ledoux, who currently resides off‑island, and board member Lewis Seau. Togiola requested that the committee be provided with all minutes related to the American250 discussions.
**CHILD SUPPORT PAYMENT BY ASTCA**
The hearing took a sharp turn when Senate President Tuaolo asked Avamua whether the board had approved $100,000 for a child support payment made on behalf of former CEO Chuck Leota to the High Court.
Avamua confirmed the payment had been made — but insisted it was not the reason he resigned.
Tuaolo pressed further: “Who approved it? Did the board approve $100,000 for Chuck’s child support?”
Former vice chair Ella Gurr responded. She explained that Leota’s severance package was under discussion, and the board had considered transitioning him into a career service position as Chief Operations Officer instead of issuing a severance payout.
She said the child support payment was raised during board discussions, but the majority of the board did not support it, and the matter was tabled.
According to Gurr, the ASTCA CEO then sought approval directly from the Governor, who approved the payment. The board only learned about it afterward.
Tuaolo asked again whether the board had approved the payment. Avamua confirmed:
“No, the board did not approve it.”
He also confirmed that the Governor had approved the payment.
Senator Togiola asked where the money came from. Avamua said the payment was issued from ASTCA’s general account, and the check was made out to the High Court of American Samoa.
Samoa News will report further in tomorrow’s issue on ASTCA CEO Folasaitu Sorepa Thomas’ answers to direct questioning that took place on Monday morning during the Fono’s joint budget hearing regarding the controversial child support payment made on behalf of former CEO Chuck Leota using ASTCA funds.

item.title: Obituaries for September 16
item.description:
David Kalani Kaili Calles, Sr., 99, of Hilo died Aug. 1 at Hale Anuenue Restorative Care Center. Born in Hilo, he was a retired clerk for Young Brothers Ltd., U.S. Army veteran trained with several bodybuilding clubs, won the title 1950 Mr. Big Island HI, coached women’s volleyball, supported and participated in Haili volleyball tournaments, served as 1952 USA Commissioner Volleyball District Hilo was co-founder of the Hilo Ohana Horseshoe Pitchers Club, former member of HSHPA and NHPA Horseshoe Pitchers associations and, in 2009, the horseshoe courts at Onekahakaha Beach Park were dedicated to him. Visitation 9-10 a.m. Monday (Sep. 21) at Dodo Mortuary Chapel. Eulogy and memories until 10:45 a.m. Burial to follow at the Hawaii Veterans Cemetery #2. Casual attire. Survived by son, David (Claudia) Calles Jr. of Hilo; daughter, Darlene (Amanda) Calles-Christian of Hilo; stepdaughters, April (Ronald) Supalo of Chicago and Louise (Cornelius) Tarr of Utah; grandchildren, great grandchildren, cousins, nieces and nephews. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

The post Obituaries for September 16 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Carrier USS Abraham Lincoln Operates with Australians in the South China Sea
item.description: USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72) recently operated with Royal Australian Navy frigates in the South China Sea, the Australian Department of Defense announced Tuesday. Frigates HMAS Perth (FFH157) and HMAS Stuart (FFH153) supported the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group during its transit of the South China Sea in accordance with international law, according to a news release. “Australian Defense Force and the U.S. routinely train and operate together, increasing interoperability between our forces and strengthening our collective capabilities,” reads the release. The news release did not disclose when the Australian frigates supported the U.S. strike group in the South China Sea.

item.title: Amata congratulates Dr. Mata’uitafā Temukisa Solomona Fai’ai on Yale Doctorate
item.description:
Washington, D.C. — Congresswoman Uifa’atali Amata congratulates Dr. Mata’uitafā Temukisa Solomona Fai’ai, Ph.D., M.P.H., on earning her doctorate in Chronic Disease Epidemiology from Yale University. Her doctoral research focused on cardiometabolic health among adolescents in American Samoa.

“Congratulations to Dr. Mata’uitafā on this outstanding academic achievement and the dedication and perseverance that brought her to this milestone,” said Congresswoman Amata. “It is especially meaningful to see a daughter of American Samoa applying her education and research to improving the health of our Samoan and Pacific communities. Her accomplishments encourage our young people to pursue their educational goals and use their talents in service to others.”

Dr. Mata’uitafā is from Leone, Tutuila; Olosega, Manu’a; and Safune, Savai’i. She earned her Ph.D. in Chronic Disease Epidemiology through the Yale Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, completing her doctoral training in the Yale School of Public Health.

She is continuing her work in Pacific public health as a Postdoctoral Fellow in the Global Health Emerging Scholars (GHES) Fellowship Program through Yale University, in collaboration with the Samoa Ministry of Health Collaborative Research Center. Her fellowship focuses on using social network analysis to understand peer influences on adolescent health and inform culturally relevant interventions addressing noncommunicable disease risk among Samoan adolescents.

“Earning a doctorate from Yale is a testament to what is possible for a girl born and raised in American Samoa: to pursue her dreams and receive a world-class education while remaining deeply rooted in her family and community,” said Dr. Mata’uitafā. “I hope my journey reflects the strength and resilience of Pasefika women, who often pursue our aspirations while caring for and uplifting our families.”

“American Samoa is proud of Dr. Mata’uitafā and all that she has accomplished,” continued Congresswoman Amata. “Her example demonstrates the importance of education, determination, and using our abilities in service to others. Fa’amalo and congratulations to Dr. Mata’uitafā and her family.”

item.title: Vaitogi ‘SA’ commences at 6 p.m.
item.description:
Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Vaitogi village will be observing and enforcing their annual curfew or "SA" for this year starting at 6:00 pm today, Tuesday, September 15, 2026, and ending at 6:00 pm on Wednesday, September 16, 2026. 

The tradition dates back over a century to 1896. 

According to historical village accounts, a massive Great Fire broke out and raged violently through Vaitogi lands for days. The fire could not be controlled, destroying scores of acres of crops, vegetation, and fales, directly threatening the lives of everyone in the village. With no physical way left to combat the flames, the village chiefs gathered all the residents together to pray for divine intervention.

Local tradition states that immediately following their unified prayers, a miraculous heavy rain fell and completely extinguished the fire. 

To honor this miracle, the village council established the first official 24-hour sā in 1897. It has been strictly observed every year since, traditionally taking place from 6:00 PM on September 15th to 6:00 PM on September 16th.

Local News

item.title: Western Pacific scientists chart research needs for reopened fisheries
item.description:
Source: Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council

HONOLULU  — The Scientific and Statistical Committee (SSC) of the Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council concluded its three-day meeting Thursday. 

For the American Samoa longline fishery, the SSC said if the Council decides to change existing turtle-related gear requirements, the Council should ask the Pacific  Islands Fisheries Science Center (PIFSC) to use observer data to evaluate potential effects on turtle interactions and on target and nontarget catch, particularly silky and oceanic whitetip sharks. 

Members highlighted that environmental changes and other basin-wide factors can also influence turtle interaction rates, complicating comparisons of fishery performance before and after gear regulations were implemented.

Reexamining Fishing Access Around Rose Atoll

The Committee also reviewed possible changes to the Large Vessel Prohibited Area (LVPA) around Muliāva (Rose Atoll), which restricts large-vessel fishing between 12 and 50 nautical miles from the atoll.

Members noted the LVPA did not prevent the decline of American Samoa’s smaller longline fleet. 

The SSC said U.S. purse seiners are unlikely to fish around Rose Atoll because of the area’s small size, although purse-seine fishing there, if it occurred, could potentially affect species targeted by the small-boat fleet. Members pointed out that large longline vessels primarily target albacore and are unlikely to compete substantially with the target species of the small-boat fleet. 

The SSC also said the South Pacific albacore stock remains healthy even as vessel numbers, participation and catch rates in the American Samoa fleet have declined.

Electronic monitoring being implemented in the longline fleet in 2027 is expected to provide additional information for evaluating fishing activity.

Looking Beyond Pounds and Dollars

Other science presented during the meeting highlighted why the effects of fishery management cannot always be measured through commercial landings alone.

PIFSC’s American Samoa Fish Flow Project found seafood from small-boat, longline and purse-seine fisheries contributes an estimated 560,000 to 859,000 meals to the local community. Small-boat catch flows extensively through families, friends, community leaders and events, with sharing often taking priority over sales. Researchers said some roadside sales, gifted fish and other forms of distribution are incompletely captured by conventional fishery statistics. 

“The value of a gifted fish likely exceeds its commercial value,” SSC member Alister Hunt said, questioning how well commercial and recreational fishery statistics capture seafood sharing and its cultural value. 

The findings complement work by the SSC’s Social Valuation Working Group, which developed four domains for considering the broader value of fisheries: food security and sovereignty, cultural importance, social cohesion, and well-being and livelihood integration. The Committee endorsed the domains for Council review.

Setting Future Research Priorities

The SSC also completed its ranking of 15 regional fishery research priorities developed with input from the Council’s Advisory Panels and Fishing Industry Advisory Committee. The priorities focus largely on evaluating fishery closures, economic and market dynamics, improving data collection and addressing depredation. The SSC recommended the Council review and adopt the final rankings. 

The Committee also recommended 2027–2030 acceptable biological catches totaling 51,510 pounds for nine American Samoa bottomfish species and endorsed the terms of reference and reviewers for the upcoming independent review of the main Hawaiian Islands deep-seven bottomfish stock assessment.

The SSC provides advice to the Council, which will meet virtually Sept. 15-17, 2026, with host sites in Hawai‘i, American Samoa, Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands. 

The Committee called for a deliberate, science-based approach as commercial fishing resumes in the NWHI. The SSC recommended forming a working group with Council and NOAA Pacific Islands Fisheries Science Center (PIFSC) staff to develop a bottomfish data collection plan. It also recommended the Council consider an experimental fishing permit (EFP) as the fishery reopens and said any longer-term permitting regime should have a clearly defined objective.

The NWHI bottomfish fishery had been closed to commercial fishing since 2010. Before closure, the area accounted for about half of Hawai‘i bottomfish management unit species landings and supplied local markets with species specifically caught there. As fishing resumes, SSC members emphasized the need to design data collection carefully to support future spatially explicit assessments. 

“An EFP may not be the quickest way to fish, but it may be the right tool to collect data at the start,” said SSC member Shelton Harley. He added that the long period with little fishing creates an opportunity to learn more about natural mortality and growth rates. 

Scientists Support Removing Outdated Swordfish Restriction

As part of its review of actions identified under the federal Executive Order on “Restoring American Seafood Competitiveness,” the SSC agreed there is no scientific basis to retain the swordfish retention limit in the Hawai‘i deep-set longline fishery. Members noted that other sea turtle mitigation measures have been implemented, circle hooks are mandatory in the fishery and the fishery will have full electronic monitoring implementation. 

The current rule limits an unobserved deep-set vessel north of the equator to 25 swordfish per trip when using circle hooks and 10 with other hooks. The restriction originated when the Hawai‘i shallow-set swordfish fishery was closed under a court order more than two decades ago, with the intent of preventing vessels engaging in deep-set fishing from transitioning to shallow-set fishing while at sea. Since the limit was last modified in 2012, deep-set vessels have averaged fewer than five swordfish per trip. 

For two other Seafood Executive Order priorities, the SSC identified analyses needed to inform the Council’s management decisions. 

For the Hawai‘i shallow-set fishery, PIFSC reported that it is developing a model to estimate loggerhead and leatherback turtle interactions with and without trip limits, with the results to inform updated population assessments. The Committee asked Council and PIFSC staff to coordinate with its protected species working group before the December meeting for updates and continued discussion of the technical analyses that will inform Council decision-making.

 In Person: (Host Site)

Online: Via Webex: https://tinyurl.com/208CouncilMtg

Event password: CM208mtg

item.title: Obituaries for September 13
item.description:
Lucila Ang Battad, 71, of Hilo died July 22 at home. Born in Manila, Philippines, she was the owner of New China Restaurant in Hilo. Visitation 9-11 a.m. Saturday (Sep. 19) at Dodo Mortuary chapel. Funeral service at 11 a.m. Burial to follow at Homelani Memorial Park. Casual attire. Survived by husband, Segundo Battad of Hilo; son, Paul (Larissa Lee) Battad of Hilo; stepson, John Cadaos of Las Vegas; stepdaughters, Marlene Battad Palas, Kay Battad Chan and Josephine Battad Arconado of Philippines, Maricar Battad of Hilo; brothers, Melchor (Lourdes) Ang, Tony Ang, Luicito Ang and Fernando Ang of Philippines; sister, Imelda Ang of Philippines; a grandson; nieces and nephews. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

The post Obituaries for September 13 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Volcano Watch: Remembering the 1919–1920 Maunaiki eruption of Kilauea
item.description:
Kilauea has drawn huge crowds to witness the lava fountaining episodes from its summit crater of Halema‘uma‘u since December 2024, with many visitors hiking trails and visiting overlooks to watch the eruption. However, there are many other trails across the unique, lava-strewn landscape of Kilauea that can be hiked during pauses between lava fountaining episodes, including the Footprints Trail.

item.title: Houthis Make Moves On Red Sea, U.S., Iran Go Tanker for Warship
item.description: The Houthis in Yemen have seized Perim Island, a parcel of land that lies in the Red Sea in an amphibious assault, giving the Iranian-backed group a strategic foothold over the Bab el-Mandeb. The Houthis’ push this week – first taking Mocha on the Red Sea’s North Coast, then Perim Island – coincides with escalating tensions between Iran and the U.S., with Washington establishing that for any warship to come under attack, it will strike an Iranian tanker. It is not immediately clear what the Houthis’ movement will mean for the ongoing U.S.-Iran war. The Yemini group shut down shipping

item.description: The following is a summary of major ship movements and exercises in the Western Pacific over the last week. In the South China Sea Aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72), cruiser USS Robert Smalls (CG-62), destroyer USS Frank E. Petersen Jr. (DDG-121) are operating in the South China Sea following their departure from Thailand on Sunday after completing a port visit. At Lumut Naval Base, Malaysia Indian Navy destroyer INS Mysore (D60) arrived Wednesday at Royal Malaysian Navy Lumut Naval Base to join RMN corvette KD Lekir (FSG26) and training ship KD Gagah Samudera (271) for exercise Samudra Laksamana 4/26.
